units.translation: There are two forms, μόλις [with difficulty] and μόγις [with difficulty], about which discussion is found in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 1128-1129, with the testimonies of the grammarians also recorded. It can be held as certain that the tragedians and in general the ancient Attic writers preferred μόλις [with difficulty], although the manuscripts not infrequently fluctuate between the two forms. In Sophocles the form μόλις [with difficulty] is constant in the Medicean codex, but in four verses of Aeschylus μόγις [with difficulty] is read twice and μόλις [with difficulty] twice.
having with difficulty persuaded my father's mind.
having crossed Thrace with difficulty with a great army.

For you have destroyed me not with difficulty (Karsten: γάρ μ᾽ [for me]) the second time, which Triclinius interprets as 'not with difficulty, but quickly', and she speaks of her own death which is about to happen. Schneidewin: 'not a little, but utterly'.

Let there be a foreign war, not with difficulty present. Where Weil says: "οὐ μόλις παρών [not with difficulty present] the scholiast well explains as οὐ μακράν [not far off], provided you take this of time. He says that an external war will easily come and is all but present." A third example of this expression is in Euripides 334 θέλουσαν οὐ μόλις καλεῖς [you call her willing, not with difficulty].

I will destroy you before my own fate. A useless verse, which I do not understand with what purpose it could have been added by Aeschylus, since it contains nothing other than the words immediately following ἴτ᾽ ἐς φθόρον πεσόντα [go to ruin, falling], which follow most aptly after v. 1265.
For the portion of tyranny is riper.
